thread.title: Why Apple Won't Be The Next BlackBerry - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Daniel Thurecht
title: Why Apple Won't Be The Next BlackBerry - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Introduction The last couple of months have been very rough on Apple’s ( AAPL ) share price, with their market capitalization falling from first place to fourth place behind Amazon ( AMZN ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOG ) ( GOOGL ). Their selloff hit an extreme point last week when their share price plunged near 10% in a single trading session after they reduced their first quarter forecast .
AAPL Market Cap data by YCharts
Could Apple Be The Next BlackBerry? Naturally this has caused concerns regarding their future to resurface, as across the last few decades there has been numerous once dominant technology firms fall from grace into obscurity. Recently there was an article published at the Motley Fool discussing whether Apple is at risk of becoming the next BlackBerry ( BB ). This caught my attention and although the author’s perspective was interesting and there wasn’t anything in particular I necessarily disagreed with, there is one massive difference between today’s Apple and yesterday’s BlackBerry that I feel wasn’t considered. Since the history of Apple and BlackBerry have been widely discussed over the years, to keep my article condensed I’ll assume the reader is already broadly aware of both companies’ stories.
BB data by YCharts
The Massive Difference Unfortunately for BlackBerry, they weren’t able to hold onto their dominant position for a great enough length of time to really capitalize and thus build a fortress of financial strength. Thankfully for Apple, they’ve maintained their dominant position to capitalize better than virtually any other in recent human history. The stark difference between today’s Apple and yesterday’s BlackBerry is easily noticeable when observing the two graphs included below. Even BlackBerry’s peak free cash flow of $2.4b in 2011 pales in comparison to Apple’s latest annual free cash flow $64.12b. On top of this, Apple is famous for holding well over $100b of cash and marketable securities net of debt, which provides another pillar to their fortress like financial position.
BB Free Cash Flow (Annual) data by YCharts BB Free Cash Flow (Annual) data by YCharts
Why This Matters Whether an individual likes it or not, money makes a massive difference in this world and Apple is the king of generating money. Even though Blackberries were once very popular, despite having their market capitalization briefly surpass $100b the company never amassed any significant earnings and financial size. On the other hand, Apple has amassed what is arguably the greatest financial strength in the corporate world that even surpasses numerous countries.
This provides Apple with the ability to essentially match or outspend their competitors if required to retain their top tier position. Although this doesn’t completely guarantee future success, when combined with their strong brand and ecosystem it forms yet another piece of the proverbial wall keeping competitors from ransacking their company.
Their insane financial strength also provides them the ability to acquire another massive company to diversify their earnings, reignite earnings growth or simply acquire new innovative competing products. Obviously any future acquisition would have to receive government approval and thus be capable of passing antitrust laws.
Currently Apple is deploying a record amount of cash through their buyback program and whilst I currently see this as a positive, if this continues in the long-term it should be monitored to ensure these don’t begin taking priority over research and development spending.
IBM Is A Better Comparison It’s my belief that the worst scenario Apple faces is a future more alike to what IBM ( IBM ) is currently fighting their way through, than that faced by BlackBerry. Whilst their products and services are vastly different, if the situation for Apple continues deteriorating their future may prove similar from a high level perspective. IBM was previously dominating their industry; however, once again technology continued marching forwards and unfortunately they failed to move quickly into new areas, such as cloud storage and thus they’ve spent the last few years struggling to regain lost ground.
Even though IBM slipped behind, their solid financial position and strong free cash flow have provided them with more options and ability to fight back and thus they haven’t ended up crushed like BlackBerry. Whether IBM’s focus on their new strategic imperatives manages to allow them to regain their former glory remains to be seen; however, it appears they’re not facing the same destiny BlackBerry has experienced. To be perfectly clear, I’m not predicting Apple will face the same problems as IBM, I’m merely saying this is the worst realistic scenario I envision. If the future proves this comparison accurate, then I would expect there to be limited further downside potential for Apple’s share price since it’s already fallen by a similar percentage as IBM’s share price.
AAPL data by YCharts
Conclusion Although it’s possible the dominance Apple has exhibited during the past decades begins to wane in the future, given their insanely strong financial position and copious free cash flow, I believe it’s extremely unlikely they’re heading in the same way as BlackBerry. If Apple has begun to lose their previously innovative way, the worst comparable scenario I envision happening is one where they follow a similar path to IBM. Since they have also developed many strong qualitative attributes, such as branding and ecosystem, this isn’t my base case scenario. Therefore, following the recent share price plunge I see limited further downside, providing the market as a whole avoids falling off a cliff.
